newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Zedillo urges peace in rebel zone.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Zedillo urges peace in rebel zone.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo, visiting a state where Marxist guerrillas fought the army last month, called on Thursday for peace and pledged to fight the region's poverty.

"Dialogue and tolerance are the only tools to resolve differences, to find responses to complaints, to advance united towards social justice," Zedillo told a predominantly Indian audience in the southwestern state of Guerrero.
"Today, when democracy is really getting stronger in Mexico, we must all reaffirm our commitment to peace and harmony," he added.

Guerrero is home to the Marxist Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), which sprang up at a peasant rally last June 28, and has launched sporadic attacks since, including two clashes with troops last month in Guerrero in which nine people died.
After Zedillo's visit, the EPR issued a communique in Acapulco, a Pacific resort some 50 miles (80 km) from Olinala, which outlined possible preconditions for stopping the conflict.

The document, signed by rebel commander Hermenegildo, called for talks between political, social and religious groups and the government -- "a wide-ranging forum of dialogue, negotiation and, above all, solutions to great shortages, demands and social backwardness."
The communique was not issued in response to Zedillo's call, however, and did not directly suggest the rebels would be willing to sit down to peace talks.

The EPR said it answered a published plea by a group of Guerrero intellectuals this week to the EPR and the army to immediately pull back fighting troops, in the hope that would set the stage for launching peace negotiations.

Zedillo was making his third visit to Guerrero this year. Officials said it was the first by a Mexican head of state to the inhospitable, arid and poor mountain region where the rebels have been most active.
At the launch of a $34 million regional aid plan in Olinala, 120 miles (180 km) south of Mexico City, Zedillo said everyone was obliged to fight poverty, regardless of their political party.

Roberto Cabrera, a local leader, welcomed the initiative but told the president more aid was needed. "We don't want to be given things for the rest of our lives," he said. "We don't want to be brought bags of corn flour or packets of milk."
